analysis.one_liner: Requires regular inspections, public inspection results, and fines for substandard Medicare hospice programs.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to inspect Medicare hospice programs and fine substandard ones cleared the House Ways and Means Committee by voice vote on December 17, 2020, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The HOSPICE Act would have required Medicare-certified hospice programs to be inspected at least every two to three years, forced the results onto a public CMS website, and created escalating penalties for programs that fail Medicare's care standards — fines of up to $10,000 per day, suspended payments, temporary management, and eventually loss of certification. It would also have run a "special focus program" with twice-yearly inspections for the worst performers and doubled the payment penalty for hospices that fail to report quality data. It died on the House calendar without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Terminally ill patients in Medicare hospice care and their families. Hospices were, by law, subject to weaker routine oversight than most other Medicare providers; the bill would have mandated recurring inspections, banned surveyors with conflicts of interest, published inspection findings online so families could check a program before enrolling a loved one, and given the government real tools — daily fines, payment suspension, temporary management, and termination — against programs providing substandard care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Terminally ill Medicare hospice patients and families

how_it_helps.text: Requires every certified hospice to undergo a standard inspection at least every 36 months, tightening to every 24 months starting October 1, 2021 — putting hospice oversight on par with the recurring surveys other Medicare providers face.
Orders CMS to publish hospice inspection reports and enforcement actions on a prominent, searchable public website starting by October 2022, so families can see a program's record before choosing it.
Creates a Special Focus Program for hospices that substantially fail Medicare standards, with inspections at least every six months until they come into compliance.

Gives CMS a graduated enforcement toolkit for deficient programs: civil monetary penalties of up to $10,000 per day of noncompliance, suspension of Medicare payments, appointment of temporary management, and termination of certification when problems immediately jeopardize patient health and safety.

Bars surveyors who worked for, consulted for, or hold a financial interest in the hospice they are inspecting, requires multidisciplinary inspection teams, and mandates comprehensive, tested surveyor training.
Doubles the payment reduction for hospices that fail to meet quality-data reporting requirements, from 2 to 4 percentage points for fiscal year 2023 onward.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare-certified hospice programs bear the direct costs: inspection-related compliance work, civil fines of up to $10,000 per day of noncompliance, and a doubled payment penalty for failing to report quality data. The Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund would transfer $10 million per year (starting fiscal 2022) to CMS to pay for the surveys. Poorly performing programs risk suspended payments or termination, which means losing Medicare revenue entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare hospice providers and the Medicare trust fund

drawbacks.text: It costs the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund $10 million per year, permanently, to fund the survey program.

The penalties are real money for providers: fines of up to $10,000 per day of noncompliance and a doubled quality-reporting payment penalty (4 percentage points from fiscal 2023) would fall on hospice programs, including small community organizations, and could push some marginal providers out of Medicare.

Tighter enforcement could reduce access to hospice care in some areas if programs close — a concern the bill itself acknowledges by requiring the Comptroller General to report within 36 months on how the new surveys and remedies affect access to and quality of hospice care.

Enforcement is not immediate even for noncompliant programs: CMS may keep paying a deficient hospice for up to six months under an approved corrective-action plan before termination, and remedies for problems not deemed 'immediate jeopardy' are discretionary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is modest and targeted: about $10 million a year in survey funding plus penalties aimed only at programs that fail Medicare's care standards, in exchange for recurring inspections and public inspection records for a service used by people at the end of life. Compliant hospices would mostly face routine inspections and paperwork; the sharpest costs — daily fines, payment suspension, termination — land on deficient programs, which is the point. The genuine uncertainty is whether stricter enforcement shrinks access to hospice care in some markets, which is why the bill directs a government study of exactly that question. On balance the design is sound, though the six-month window for continuing payments to noncompliant programs softens the teeth.

outcome.mechanism: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the bill by voice vote and it was placed on the House calendar on December 17, 2020, but the House never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jimmy Panetta (D-CA) introduced the bill on February 10, 2020 with Reps. Tom Reed (R-NY) and Brian Higgins (D-NY); it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, in part, to Energy and Commerce.
On February 12, 2020, the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health held a markup and ordered the bill reported as amended by voice vote — a vote with no recorded opposition.

The bill then sat for ten months. On December 17, 2020 — the final weeks of the congressional session — the full Ways and Means Committee formally reported it with an amendment (House Report 116-660, Part I), the Energy and Commerce Committee was discharged, and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 544, the step before a floor vote.
Representatives Dan Kildee (D-MI) and Tom Rice (R-SC) added their support on the day of the committee report, keeping the sponsorship split evenly between the parties.
No floor vote ever came. The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and all bills not passed by then die automatically; the bill would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare-certified hospice programs are better off: no recurring inspection mandate, no public posting of inspection results, and no exposure to daily fines, payment suspension, or termination for deficient care. Patients and families gained nothing because the bill never reached the floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospice providers spared inspections, fines, and termination

industries.note: The bill subjects hospices to recurring federal inspections, public disclosure of inspection results, fines of up to $10,000 per day of noncompliance, payment suspension, temporary management, and termination for programs that fail Medicare's care standards — and doubles the payment penalty for failing to report quality data. Substandard programs lose revenue and, in the worst cases, their certification; patients and families get enforceable quality standards and public records to check before enrolling.

The bill formally extends approved national accreditation bodies' survey authority to hospice programs (mirroring home health agencies) and makes them part of the inspection system, requiring them to submit survey and enforcement data to CMS and to use trained surveyors. They gain a permanent, federally sanctioned role in hospice oversight.
